This is my temporary description of the website, which will contain r code relevant to the Data 200 class
Always run your libraries each time you start working on a document, whether its the first time you’re opening it or if you’re reopening it

#Example for if you're using the tidyverse and bayesrules packages
library(tidyverse)
library(bayesrules)

If you get an error that says that the package can’t be found, make sure they are installed

#Example for installing tidyverse and bayesrules packages
install.packages("tidyverse")
install.packages("bayesrules")

title: Scatterplots
text:
A scatter plot can be used to plot two numeric variables

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep)) +
  geom_point()








You can add a color to represent one categorical variable

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = bill_len, y = bill_dep, color = species)) +
  geom_point()

title: Histograms
text:
A histogram can be used to plot one numeric variable

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = flipper_len)) +
  geom_histogram()








You can add color to represent one categorical variable

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram()








Customize the histogram by adding the ‘bins’ argument

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = flipper_len, fill = species)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20)

title: Bar Graphs
text:
A bar graph can be used to represent the count of one categorical variable

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = island)) +
  geom_bar()








You can add a fill to represent a second categorical variable

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar()

title: Box Plots
text:
A box plot can be used to show the distribution of one numeric variable

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = body_mass)) +
  geom_boxplot()








To add a categorical variable, you can add it to the aes function

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = body_mass, y = species)) +
  geom_boxplot()

title: Operators
text:
The Assignment Operator
This operator creates or edits objects in the R environment tab. These can store any information that R outputs

glimpse(my_thing) #I can't see anything because there isn't anything called 'my_thing'

Error:
! object 'my_thing' not found



my_thing <- c(1, 3, 5, 7) #Storing the numbers 1, 3, 5, and 7 in an object called "my_thing"

glimpse(my_thing) #Now, I can see my list of numbers

 num [1:4] 1 3 5 7

title: Loading/Viewing my Data
text:
There are many different ways of viewing a dataset
data("penguins") #loading the penguins dataset that is included in R
glimpse() shows all of the variables and their R variable type
glimpse(penguins)

Rows: 344
Columns: 8
$ species     <fct> Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Ad…
$ island      <fct> Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Tor…
$ bill_len    <dbl> 39.1, 39.5, 40.3, NA, 36.7, 39.3, 38.9, 39.2, 34.1, 42.0, …
$ bill_dep    <dbl> 18.7, 17.4, 18.0, NA, 19.3, 20.6, 17.8, 19.6, 18.1, 20.2, …
$ flipper_len <int> 181, 186, 195, NA, 193, 190, 181, 195, 193, 190, 186, 180,…
$ body_mass   <int> 3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, 4250, …
$ sex         <fct> male, female, female, NA, female, male, female, male, NA, …
$ year        <int> 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007…
head() takes the top 6 rows from the dataset and displays it like a normal table, tail() does the same from the bottom
head(penguins)

  species    island bill_len bill_dep flipper_len body_mass    sex year
1  Adelie Torgersen     39.1     18.7         181      3750   male 2007
2  Adelie Torgersen     39.5     17.4         186      3800 female 2007
3  Adelie Torgersen     40.3     18.0         195      3250 female 2007
4  Adelie Torgersen       NA       NA          NA        NA   <NA> 2007
5  Adelie Torgersen     36.7     19.3         193      3450 female 2007
6  Adelie Torgersen     39.3     20.6         190      3650   male 2007
nrow() and ncol() will tell you how many rows and columns respectively are in the data
nrow(penguins) #Returns the number of rows in the penguins data

[1] 344
ncol(penguins) #Returns the number of columns

[1] 8

title: Vectors and Data Frames
text:
Vectors
A vector can be created to store a list of anything

c(23, 53, 28, 87)

[1] 23 53 28 87



c("red", "yellow", "blue", "green")

[1] "red"    "yellow" "blue"   "green" 



You can save a vector the same way as anything else in R

some_numbers <- c(23, 53, 28, 87)

cool_colors <- c("red", "yellow", "blue", "green")


glimpse(cool_colors)

 chr [1:4] "red" "yellow" "blue" "green"

glimpse(some_numbers)

 num [1:4] 23 53 28 87



You can run functions on your saved vectors

mean(some_numbers)

[1] 47.75

title: Vectors and Data Frames
text:
Data Frames
You can create a table by combining two vectors with the data.frame() function

data.frame(cool_colors, some_numbers)

  cool_colors some_numbers
1         red           23
2      yellow           53
3        blue           28
4       green           87



You can specify new names for the columns if you want

data.frame(color = cool_colors, number = some_numbers)

   color number
1    red     23
2 yellow     53
3   blue     28
4  green     87

title: Summary Stats
text:
Categorical Variables
To count each outcome in a categorical variable, you can simply use count

count(penguins, sex) #Counts the number of times each outcome occurred

     sex   n
1 female 165
2   male 168
3   <NA>  11


To get proportions as well as count, use the tabyl function

tabyl(penguins, sex)

    sex   n    percent valid_percent
 female 165 0.47965116     0.4954955
   male 168 0.48837209     0.5045045
   <NA>  11 0.03197674            NA

title: Summary Stats
text:
Numeric Variables
Most numeric summary stat functions are very intuitive

#Examples for the bill depth variable in penguins
#na.rm is added to each since they will not work if nas are included

mean(penguins$bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE) #Gives the mean

[1] 17.15117

median(penguins$bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE) #Gives the median

[1] 17.3

sd(penguins$bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE) #Gives the standard deviation

[1] 1.974793

var(penguins$bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE) #Gives the variance

[1] 3.899808

quantile(penguins$bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE) #Gives the min, Q1, Q2, Q3, and max

  0%  25%  50%  75% 100% 
13.1 15.6 17.3 18.7 21.5 




To make computing multiple summary stats at once easier, you can use the summarize function

summarize(
  penguins,
  mean(bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE),
  median(bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE),
  sd(bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) # Gives the mean, median, and standard deviation together

  mean(bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE) median(bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE)
1                     17.15117                           17.3
  sd(bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE)
1                   1.974793



Give the output better looking names by adding a name before each argument

summarize(
  penguins,
  mean_depth = mean(bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE),
  median_depth = median(bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE),
  standard_deviation = sd(bill_dep, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) #Gives the same numbers, but now has better names

  mean_depth median_depth standard_deviation
1   17.15117         17.3           1.974793

title: Bar Plots
text:
Normal Bar Plot
A bar plot can be used to represent the count of one categorical variable

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = island)) +
  geom_bar()








You can add a fill to represent a second categorical variable

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar()

title: Bar Plots
text:
Dodged Bar Plot
A dodged Bar Plot can be used to represent two categorical variables

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")

title: Bar Plots
text:
Standardized Bar Plot
A standardized bar plot can be used to represent two categorical variables, but it shows only the proportions of the fill variable within the x variable

ggplot(data = penguins, aes(x = island, fill = species)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill")
